lessons.title: Muscles produce force
lessons.text: Skeletal muscles contract to produce movement and help maintain posture. Connective tissue transfers that tension to tendons and bone. An exercise can involve both muscles that move a joint and muscles that stabilize it.
lessons.question: What can skeletal muscles do?
choices: Produce force and help stabilize posture
Only move joints; never stabilize them
Connect bone to bone without contracting
lessons.explanation: Muscle contractions can create movement or help hold a position.

lessons.title: Tendons transfer force
lessons.text: Tendons are dense connective tissue that connect muscle to bone. They transmit muscle tension. Selecting a painful region does not identify which tissue is involved; record what you experience and any restrictions supplied by your clinician.
lessons.question: What is a tendon's main connection?
lessons.explanation: Tendons connect muscle to bone; ligaments typically connect bones at joints.

lessons.title: Ligaments support joints
lessons.text: Ligaments connect bones and help support joints. They are connective tissue, not muscles. Knowing a ligament's location does not establish a diagnosis or readiness to return to training.
lessons.question: Which description fits a ligament?
choices: A connection from muscle to bone
lessons.explanation: Ligaments join bones and contribute to joint support.

lessons.title: Joints connect the skeleton
lessons.text: A joint is where skeletal elements meet. Joints differ in structure and how much movement they allow. A body-region diagram is a navigation aid, not an assessment of an individual's joint or range of motion.
lessons.question: Do all joints permit the same amount of movement?
choices: No; their structure and permitted movement differ
lessons.explanation: Joints are classified by structure and function, including their degree of movement.

lessons.title: What does the evidence actually support?
lessons.text: Currier and colleagues compared resistance-training prescriptions in healthy adults in a 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis. Many prescriptions improved strength and muscle size. This research compares load, sets and frequency; it does not establish which exercise is safest for your injury or prove one exercise is best for everyone.
lessons.question: Can this healthy-adult training review establish the safest exercise for an individual injury?
choices: No; that claim goes beyond the studied question
Yes, if an exercise ranks first
lessons.explanation: Check the population, outcome and comparison before applying a study to a personal decision.
lessons.sourceLabel: Currier et al., BJSM (2023), systematic review and network meta-analysis
